cur:catacombs-ponziano-bust-of-christ.summary: Christ appears as a frontal bust with a cross-nimbus, large eyes, short beard and long hair, set within an arched frame above a painted inscription. The austere, hieratic face belongs to the age of icons and shows how the catacombs continued to be decorated for pilgrims long after burials there had ceased.
facts: Commons dates the painting to about the 6th–7th century, from Wilpert's 1903 plate.
The Catacomb of Pontian, on the Via Portuense, is also known for a painted baptistery and frescoes of the martyrs Abdon and Sennen.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

cur:manuscripts-ramsey-psalter-crucifixi.summary: In delicate tinted line drawing, Christ hangs dead on the cross, his head sunk on his shoulder, beneath the inscription 'Hic est Nazarenus rex Iudeorum'; the Virgin, at left, raises her veil to her weeping face, and John, at right, writes on a scroll while gazing up at him. The fluttering drapery and fine, nervous line make this one of the most moving images in Anglo-Saxon art.
facts: Wikipedia notes that this coloured outline drawing draws on the style of the Utrecht Psalter, which was then in England.
The same artist seems to have worked at Fleury Abbey and at Saint-Bertin, Saint-Omer, where he contributed to the Boulogne Gospels.
The psalter's script inspired the 'foundational hand' of the 20th-century calligrapher Edward Johnston.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-71-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos sits in a globe-mandorla on a mountain top with a book on his knee and tramples the 'oppressor' of the psalm, while angels hold the moon and the sun and a wreath hangs above. Around him kings bring gifts and the poor are rescued. This royal psalm, with its 'kings of Tarshish ... shall bring presents', was read of the Magi and of Christ's reign.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-71-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-naples-baptistery-peter-o.summary: A haloed, beardless Christ in white stands at the left, turned towards a blue sea full of fish, where a figure in the water reaches towards him; above, a man sits in a boat. The incomplete scene has been read as the Miraculous Draught of Fishes, as Christ saving Peter from the waves, or as the calling of Peter and Andrew.
facts: Of the scenes once set within garlands around the dome, four survive: the Traditio Legis, the Samaritan woman with the Wedding at Cana, the Miraculous Draught (or Peter on the water), and the women at the tomb.

The baptistery of San Giovanni in Fonte beside Naples Cathedral is one of the oldest in the West; its building is dated to the 4th century, and its construction is attributed to Bishop Severus (362–408) or to later bishops.

links.label: Wikipedia: Battistero di San Giovanni in Fonte (Napoli)
Wikimedia Commons: Mosaics in the Battistero di San Giovanni in Fonte (Naples)

cur:monumental-naples-baptistery-peter-o.notes: The exact Gospel episode is uncertain; scholars propose the Miraculous Draught, Peter walking on the water, a combination of both, or the calling of Peter and Andrew.

Q87665248.summary: Under a pierced arch the central panel shows the Nativity: the Virgin reclines beside the manger where the swaddled Christ Child lies with the ox and ass, angels crowd above, and in the foreground the newborn is bathed. The wings continue the story of Christ's victory in small, crowded scenes, among them the Entry into Jerusalem, the Descent into Limbo and the Ascension. A portable triptych like this gathered the great feasts into a single object for private prayer.
facts: Greek inscriptions name the scenes: the Nativity at the centre, the Entry into Jerusalem and the Descent into Limbo on the left wing, and the Ascension on the right.
The Louvre dates the triptych to 950–1000 on stylistic grounds and places it in Constantinople under the Macedonian dynasty.
It passed through the collections of Prince Alexis Soltykoff (sold 1861), Frédéric Spitzer and Edmond Foulc before the Louvre bought it from Raoul Duseigneur in 1900.
Q87665248.notes: Original title: Triptyque : la Nativité (OA 5004). The Louvre's date text reads '2e moitié du Xe siècle'.

walters:W.44.26V.summary: The apostles crowd in two groups around the Virgin, faces and hands lifted toward the sky, while at the top of the gold ground only the feet and the hem of Christ's robe remain visible as he disappears into a band of blue cloud. Showing only the vanishing feet lets the viewer share the witnesses' upward gaze. The Virgin, veiled and haloed at the centre, anchors the scene as the mother who remains with the infant Church.
facts: This is one of ten full-page miniatures added in the 14th century as a prefatory cycle to a Psalter made in French Flanders c. 1250–1275 for a woman with Cistercian connections.
The cycle runs in facing pairs with blank backs, from the Annunciation (fol. 18v) to Pentecost (fol. 27r); the Ascension is on fol. 26v.
Because the leaves have blank backs, each miniature faces its partner across an opening; the Ascension (fol. 26v) faces Pentecost (fol. 27r).

links.label: The Digital Walters: Psalter for a Cistercian woman (W.44)

walters:W.44.26V.notes: The Walters online record dates this leaf with the whole manuscript to the third quarter of the 13th century, but the Walters' own manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters) states that the ten full-page miniatures of the prefatory cycle (fols. 18v–27r) were added in the fourteenth century; the date is corrected accordingly. The worklist year (750) was a parsing error.

commons:132629185.summary: Over the doors of a great pilgrimage church, Christ the Judge sits enthroned in a starry mandorla, his right hand raised toward the saved and his left lowered toward the damned. Around him 124 figures act out the drama of the end of time — the procession of saints into the heavenly Jerusalem on one side, the chaos of hell on the other. It confronted every pilgrim with the promise and warning of Christ's return.
facts: Conques lay on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, and the tympanum greeted the many pilgrims who came to venerate the relics of Saint Foy.
Latin verse inscriptions on the bands summarize the message, ending with a warning that sinners will face a harsh judgment unless they amend their ways.
Small figures peeking over the frame, known as 'les curieux', seem to watch the Judgment as onlookers.
Small traces of the original paint survive, showing that the scene was once brightly coloured.
